claim: Gulf toadfish produce two main types of vocalizations with pulse repetition rates (PRRs) in the range of ~200–250 Hz – broadband agonistic grunts and multiharmonic advertisement calls known as boatwhistles.
source: Gulf toadfish (Opsanus beta), the species studied here, which produce two main types of vocalizations with pulse repetition rates (PRRs) in the range of ~200–250 Hz – broadband agonistic grunts and multiharmonic advertisement calls known as boatwhistles (Figure 1a, Tavolga, 1958; Winn, 1967; Maruska and Mensinger, 2009; Elemans et al., 2014; Bass et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to multiple published studies (Tavolga, 1958; Winn, 1967; Maruska and Mensinger, 2009; Elemans et al., 2014; Bass et al., 2015) and reference to Figure 1a showing the vocalizations.

claim: Individual VOC potentials arise from synchronous motoneuron activity in the midline vocal motor nucleus (VMN) and are matched 1:1 with individual motoneuron action potentials.
source: Individual VOC potentials arise from synchronous motoneuron activity in the midline vocal motor nucleus (VMN) and are matched 1:1 with individual motoneuron action potentials (APs) (Figure 1c; Bass and Baker, 1990; Chagnaud et al., 2012; Chagnaud and Bass, 2014)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior studies (Bass and Baker, 1990; Chagnaud et al., 2012; Chagnaud and Bass, 2014) and reference to Figure 1c showing the correlation.

claim: Each individual VOC potential represents the synchronous activity of VMN motoneurons.
source: Each individual VOC potential represents the synchronous activity of VMN motoneurons; variable potential amplitude reflects different levels of synchronous motoneuron firing and motoneuron recruitment (Figure 1c; Chagnaud et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Chagnaud et al., 2012 and reference to Figure 1c.

claim: Variable VOC potential amplitude reflects different levels of synchronous motoneuron firing and motoneuron recruitment.
source: Each individual VOC potential represents the synchronous activity of VMN motoneurons; variable potential amplitude reflects different levels of synchronous motoneuron firing and motoneuron recruitment (Figure 1c; Chagnaud et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Chagnaud et al., 2012 and reference to Figure 1c.

claim: Motoneurons possess 3–5 main dendritic branches and an axon arising from a primary dendrite or soma that lacks collaterals.
source: Motoneurons possess 3–5 main dendritic branches and an axon arising from a primary dendrite or soma that lacks collaterals and exits the brain ipsilaterally via the vocal tract (VoTr, Figure 1d, e) and joins the ipsilateral vocal nerve root (Bass and Baker, 1990; Chagnaud and Bass, 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Bass and Baker, 1990 and Chagnaud and Bass, 2014, and reference to Figure 1d, e.

claim: Each VMN is bilaterally innervated by adjacent vocal pacemaker neurons (VPN) that provide coherent excitatory input and determine VMN firing rate that directly translates into PRR or F0.
source: Each VMN is bilaterally innervated by adjacent vocal pacemaker neurons (VPN, Figure 1d, e) that provide coherent excitatory input and determine VMN firing rate that directly translates into PRR or F0 (see above) (Bass and Baker, 1990; Chagnaud et al., 2011; Chagnaud and Bass, 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Bass and Baker, 1990; Chagnaud et al., 2011; Chagnaud and Bass, 2014, and reference to Figure 1d, e.

claim: Both VPN and VMN receive input from a more rostral vocal prepacemaker nucleus (VPP) that encodes call duration.
source: Both VPN and VMN receive input from a more rostral vocal prepacemaker nucleus (VPP, Figure 1e) that encodes call duration (Chagnaud et al., 2011; Chagnaud and Bass, 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Chagnaud et al., 2011 and Chagnaud and Bass, 2014, and reference to Figure 1e.

claim: Pappas and Bennett discovered the VMN and showed the contribution of electrotonic coupling to motoneuronal synchrony.
source: Pappas and Bennett discovered the VMN (Pappas and Bennett, 1966) and showed, along with studies of electric fish (Bennett, 1971), the contribution of electrotonic coupling to motoneuronal synchrony.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Pappas and Bennett, 1966 and Bennett, 1971.

claim: Ultrastructure evidence shows gap junction contacts between VMN motoneurons and axons of unidentified origin (likely VPN).
source: This included ultrastructure evidence for gap junction contacts between VMN motoneurons and axons of unidentified origin (likely VPN) (Pappas and Bennett, 1966; also see Bass and Marchaterre, 1989).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Pappas and Bennett, 1966 and Bass and Marchaterre, 1989.

claim: Vocal nerve labeling with gap junction impassable tracers only leads to dense retrograde labeling of the ipsilateral VMN.
source: More recent studies show that vocal nerve labeling with gap junction impassable tracers only leads to dense retrograde labeling of the ipsilateral VMN, while gap junction passable tracers lead to dense transneuronal, bilateral labeling of VMN, VPN, and VPP (e.g., see Figure 1d; Bass et al., 1994; Chagnaud and Bass, 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Bass et al., 1994 and Chagnaud and Bass, 2014, and reference to Figure 1d.

claim: Gap junction passable tracers lead to dense transneuronal, bilateral labeling of VMN, VPN, and VPP.
source: More recent studies show that vocal nerve labeling with gap junction impassable tracers only leads to dense retrograde labeling of the ipsilateral VMN, while gap junction passable tracers lead to dense transneuronal, bilateral labeling of VMN, VPN, and VPP (e.g., see Figure 1d; Bass et al., 1994; Chagnaud and Bass, 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Bass et al., 1994 and Chagnaud and Bass, 2014, and reference to Figure 1d.

claim: Pappas and Bennett speculated that inhibitory input to the VMN arose from recurrent inhibitory activity.
source: Besides electrotonic coupling, Pappas and Bennett, 1966 speculated that inhibitory input to the VMN arose from recurrent inhibitory activity (antidromic stimulation of vocal nerve led to hyperpolarization (HYP) at high, but not low, stimulation amplitudes).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Pappas and Bennett, 1966.

claim: Antidromic stimulation of vocal nerve led to hyperpolarization (HYP) at high, but not low, stimulation amplitudes.
source: Besides electrotonic coupling, Pappas and Bennett, 1966 speculated that inhibitory input to the VMN arose from recurrent inhibitory activity (antidromic stimulation of vocal nerve led to hyperpolarization (HYP) at high, but not low, stimulation amplitudes).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Pappas and Bennett, 1966.

claim: A subset of glycinergic VPN neurons are transneuronally labeled with the gap junction passable tracer neurobiotin.
source: We also recently reported in Gulf toadfish a subset of glycinergic VPN neurons transneuronally labeled with the gap junction passable tracer neurobiotin, strongly suggestive of electrotonic coupling within the vocal network (Rosner et al., 2018; see Figure 1f).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Rosner et al., 2018 and reference to Figure 1f.

claim: Midbrain stimulation led to membrane depolarizations in motoneurons that increased in amplitude until a single AP was fired.
source: Midbrain stimulation led to membrane depolarizations in motoneurons that increased in amplitude until a single AP was fired (Figure 2a1, 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by reference to Figure 2a1, 2 showing the experimental data.

claim: The first AP coincided with the first appearance of a strong post-spiking HYP and a single VOC nerve potential.
source: This AP coincided with the first appearance of a strong post-spiking HYP and a single VOC nerve potential.
evidence: The claim is based on observations from the experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: With increasing stimulus strength, additional APs were detected that matched 1:1 with additional VOC potentials.
source: With increasing stimulus strength, additional APs were detected that matched 1:1 with additional VOC potentials (Figure 2a3, 4).
evidence: The claim is supported by reference to Figure 2a3, 4 showing the experimental data.

claim: Each repetitive series of VOC potentials mimicked the temporal properties of sound pulses comprising natural grunts.
source: Each repetitive series of VOC potentials mimicked the temporal properties of sound pulses comprising natural grunts (see Figure 1a; Tavolga, 1958; Winn, 1967; Maruska and Mensinger, 2009; Elemans et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Tavolga, 1958; Winn, 1967; Maruska and Mensinger, 2009; Elemans et al., 2014, and reference to Figure 1a.

claim: Across repetitions, the amplitude of the second VOC potential always exceeded the first (73.89 ± 4.4 µV vs. 36.6 ± 4.1 µV; n = 14 neurons; N = 4 fish; p<0.0001).
source: Across repetitions, the amplitude of the second VOC potential always exceeded the first (73.89 ± 4.4 µV vs. 36.6 ± 4.1 µV; n = 14 neurons; N = 4 fish; p<0.0001) (Figure 2a3–5).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data (p<0.0001) and reference to Figure 2a3–5.

claim: The reduced amplitude of the first VOC potential reflected a less synchronous and/or a partial activation of the motoneuron population.
source: The reduced amplitude of the first VOC potential reflected a less synchronous and/or a partial activation of the motoneuron population (Figure 2a3).
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the experimental data shown in Figure 2a3.

claim: The first and last VOC potentials generally showed activity distributed over a broader time course.
source: The first and last VOC potentials generally showed activity distributed over a broader time course (Figure 2b; also see inset, amplifying end of vocal nerve recording, e.g., of 'weak' synchrony).
evidence: The claim is supported by reference to Figure 2b showing the experimental data.

claim: The amplitude of the first and last VOC potentials directly reflected the extent of synchronous motoneuron activation.
source: The amplitude of the first and last VOC potentials thus directly reflected the extent of synchronous motoneuron activation.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the experimental observations.

claim: Intracellular motoneuron recordings showed broad depolarizations often present during the first and last VMN APs that often displayed spikelets strongly indicative of asynchronous motoneuron activity.
source: Intracellular motoneuron recordings showed broad depolarizations often present during the first and last VMN APs (Figure 2a3–5, b ) that often displayed spikelets strongly indicative of asynchronous motoneuron activity (Figure 2a4, b, c) (also see Chagnaud et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by reference to Figure 2a3–5, b, c showing the experimental data and citation to Chagnaud et al., 2012.

claim: The first APs had significantly wider half-widths than subsequent APs (first AP half width: 0.81 ± 0.11 ms vs. second 0.62 ± 0.06 ms; n = 8, N = 3; p=0.001).
source: These were significantly wider than those of subsequent APs whose amplitude correlated with a higher amplitude in the corresponding VOC potential (first AP half width: 0.81 ± 0.11 ms vs. second 0.62 ± 0.06 ms; n = 8, N = 3; p=0.001).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data (p=0.001).

claim: Larger, sharp-peaked VOC potential amplitudes are indicative of synchronous firing across the VMN population and correlated with narrower motoneuron APs.
source: As highlighted in Figure 2b (but also evident in Figure 2a4, c), larger, sharp-peaked VOC potential amplitudes (blue trace) are indicative of synchronous firing across the VMN population and correlated with narrower motoneuron APs (blue trace).
evidence: The claim is supported by reference to Figure 2b, 2a4, c showing the experimental data.

claim: Antidromic activation via the vocal nerve revealed motoneuron APs lacking the prominent HYP at their respective threshold.
source: Antidromic activation via the vocal nerve (electrodes implanted in vocal muscles; see Materials and methods) revealed motoneuron APs lacking the prominent HYP at their respective threshold (blue trace, Figure 2c, right).
evidence: The claim is supported by reference to Figure 2c showing the experimental data.

claim: Intracellular square pulse current injections showed no clear HYP after AP firing.
source: This was consistent with intracellular square pulse current injections showing no clear HYP after AP firing (Figure 2d).
evidence: The claim is supported by reference to Figure 2d showing the experimental data.

claim: Motoneuron AP and HYP amplitudes (relative to resting membrane potential) were significantly larger during VOC activity than following antidromic activation at threshold for AP firing (AP: vocal 29.13 ± 1.48 mV vs. antidromic: 21.46 ± 2.93 mV; p=0.024; HYP: vocal −10.92 ± 1.16 mV vs. antidromic −2.95 ± 0.70 mV; n = 12, N = 5: p=0.001).
source: Motoneuron AP and HYP amplitudes (relative to resting membrane potential [RMP]) were significantly larger during VOC activity than following antidromic activation at threshold for AP firing (AP: vocal 29.13 ± 1.48 mV vs. antidromic: 21.46 ± 2.93 mV; p=0.024; HYP: vocal −10.92 ± 1.16 mV vs. antidromic −2.95 ± 0.70 mV; n = 12, N = 5: p=0.001, see Figure 2c).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data (p=0.024 and p=0.001) and reference to Figure 2c.

claim: At low amplitudes of antidromic stimulation, small depolarizations were detected whose amplitude gradually increased with stimulation strength, with shapes and peak latencies indicative of electrotonic coupling (3.54 ± 0.28 ms; n = 9, N = 4).
source: At low amplitudes, we detected small depolarizations (Figure 3) whose amplitude gradually increased with stimulation strength, that is, with increasing recruitment of motoneuron axons and with shapes and peak latencies indicative of electrotonic coupling (3.54 ± 0.28 ms; n = 9, N = 4).
evidence: The claim is supported by reference to Figure 3 showing the experimental data.

claim: Collision experiments using antidromic-activated and intracellular-evoked APs revealed these APs could not be blocked, indicating they resulted from electrical coupling.
source: Collision experiments using antidromic-activated and intracellular-evoked APs (via intracellular current injection) revealed these APs could not be blocked, that is, they resulted from electrical coupling (Pappas and Bennett, 1966; Kiehn and Tresch, 2002, Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Pappas and Bennett, 1966 and Kiehn and Tresch, 2002, and reference to Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: With increasing amplitude of vocal nerve stimulation, the axon of the respectively recorded motoneuron was eventually recruited and an antidromic AP invaded the recorded motoneuron with a significantly shorter peak latency (1.42 ± 0.31 ms after stimulation; n = 11, N = 4) compared to the subthreshold depolarization (p=0.003).
source: With increasing amplitude of vocal nerve stimulation, the axon of the respectively recorded motoneuron was eventually recruited and an antidromic AP invaded the recorded motoneuron as shown by the significantly shorter peak latency (1.42 ± 0.31 ms after stimulation; n = 11, N = 4) compared to the previously mentioned subthreshold depolarization (p=0.003) (Figure 3).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data (p=0.003) and reference to Figure 3.

claim: Antidromic APs showed no HYP, but instead were characterized by a slow decay (double exponential fit; average time constant τ1: 0.89 ± 0.25; time constant τ2: 7.76 ± 2.48; n = 5, N = 2) back to the RMP.
source: These APs showed no HYP, but instead were characterized by a slow decay (double exponential fit; average time constant τ1: 0.89 ± 0.25; time constant τ2: 7.76 ± 2.48; n = 5, N = 2) back to the RMP (example shown in magenta trace in Figure 3a).
evidence: The claim is supported by reference to Figure 3a showing the experimental data.

claim: The AP and HYP peak amplitudes increased with stimulation strength until each reached a plateau.
source: The AP and HYP peak amplitudes increased with stimulation strength until each reached a plateau (Figure 3a).
evidence: The claim is supported by reference to Figure 3a showing the experimental data.

claim: A HYP was never observed during intracellular square pulse current injections.
source: A HYP was never observed during intracellular square pulse current injections (Figure 2d), raising the question on the origin of this HYP.
evidence: The claim is supported by reference to Figure 2d showing the experimental data.

claim: Phase plane plots revealed an additional component: a broadening of the depolarization after AP firing.
source: Phase plane plots further revealed an additional component: a broadening of the depolarization after AP firing (magenta arrows, (Figure 3a)).
evidence: The claim is supported by reference to Figure 3a showing the experimental data.

claim: A Renshaw cell-like recurrent inhibition could be ruled out as the origin of the HYP given the lack of motoneuron axon collaterals and the rapid onset of the HYP.
source: A Renshaw cell-like recurrent inhibition in which spinal motoneurons use an axon collateral to activate a local inhibitory circuit (Renshaw, 1941; Eccles et al., 1954), comparable to the 'apparently recurrent inhibition' proposed by Pappas and Bennett, 1966 to account for inhibitory input to the VMN, could be ruled out as the origin of the HYP given the lack of motoneuron axon collaterals (Figure 1d, Chagnaud and Bass, 2014) and the rapid onset of the HYP.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from anatomical observations (lack of axon collaterals) and physiological data (rapid HYP onset), supported by citations to Renshaw, 1941; Eccles et al., 1954; Pappas and Bennett, 1966; Chagnaud and Bass, 2014, and reference to Figure 1d.

claim: There was no difference in HYP amplitude (% of baseline) between cut and uncut recordings during VOCs (before cut: −8.21 ± 3.1 mV vs. after: −7.51 ± 1.22 mV; n = 18, N = 2: p=0.8).
source: There was no difference in HYP amplitude (% of baseline) between cut and uncut recordings during VOCs (before cut: −8.21 ± 3.1 mV vs. after: −7.51 ± 1.22 mV; n = 18, N = 2: p=0.8) (Figure 3—figure supplement 2)
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data (p=0.8) and reference to Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: There was no difference in HYP amplitude during antidromic stimulation after dorsal root cut (before cut: −3.2 ± 0.59 mV vs. after: −4.84 ± 0.71 mV, n = 18, N = 2: p=0.117).
source: or during antidromic stimulation (before cut: −3.2 ± 0.59 mV vs. after: −4.84 ± 0.71 mV, n = 18, N = 2: p=0.117).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data (p=0.117).

claim: These results excluded a motoneuronal collateral via one of the dorsal roots as the origin of the HYP.
source: These results excluded a motoneuronal collateral via one of the dorsal roots as the origin of the HYP.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the experimental results showing no difference in HYP after dorsal root cut.

claim: Contralateral antidromic stimulation revealed electrotonic potentials whose amplitude depended on stimulation strength.
source: Contralateral antidromic stimulation also revealed electrotonic potentials whose amplitude depended on stimulation strength (ad-contra, red traces; Figure 3a).
evidence: The claim is supported by reference to Figure 3a showing the experimental data.

claim: The peak latency of contralaterally evoked APs was significantly longer (3.47 ± 0.16 ms; n = 11, N = 4; p=0.004) than ones elicited ipsilaterally.
source: The peak latency of these APs was significantly longer (3.47 ± 0.16 ms; n = 11, N = 4; p=0.004) than ones elicited ipsilaterally (Figure 3b)
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data (p=0.004) and reference to Figure 3b.

claim: The peak latency of the ipsilaterally evoked subthreshold depolarization did not differ from contralateral, consistent with their common origin from electrotonic coupling.
source: while the peak latency of the ipsilaterally evoked subthreshold depolarization did not differ, consistent with their common origin from electrotonic coupling (see above).
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the experimental data showing similar latencies.

claim: Electrical coupling alone is able to drive AP firing, independent of whether motoneurons belong to the ipsilateral or contralateral VMN population.
source: As tract tracing and intracellular neuron fills showed that motoneurons only innervate the ipsilateral muscle (Chagnaud and Bass, 2014), electrical coupling alone is thus able to drive AP firing, independent of whether motoneurons belong to the ipsilateral or contralateral VMN population.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from anatomical data (motoneurons only innervate ipsilateral muscle) and physiological observations, supported by citation to Chagnaud and Bass, 2014.

claim: An HYP component could clearly be distinguished in the contralateral antidromic stimulation experiments.
source: As with the ipsilateral antidromic activation, an HYP component could clearly be distinguished in the contralateral antidromic stimulation experiments (Figure 4a).
evidence: The claim is supported by reference to Figure 4a showing the experimental data.

claim: The HYP occurred independent of AP firing, emphasizing the independence of the two events within a given motoneuron.
source: This HYP occurred independent of AP firing, emphasizing the independence of the two events within a given motoneuron.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the experimental observations.

claim: Intracellular current injections failed to initiate an AP in most cases, even at high current intensities (>5 nA).
source: Consistent with our findings in the closely related midshipman toadfish, Porichthys notatus (Chagnaud et al., 2012), the ability to initiate an AP via electrotonic coupling was in strong contrast to our intracellular current injections that failed to initiate an AP in most cases, even at high current intensities (>5 nA).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Chagnaud et al., 2012 and experimental observations.

claim: In cases where intracellular current injection elicited an AP, motoneurons showed rapid adaptation of AP firing, likely due to weak somatic repolarization ability.
source: In cases where intracellular current injection elicited an AP, motoneurons showed rapid adaptation of AP firing, likely due to weak somatic repolarization ability (see Figure 2d).
evidence: The claim is based on inference from experimental observations shown in Figure 2d.

claim: Motoneurons showed no signs of AP adaptation to pulse trains with brief (<5 ms) pulses, indicating the necessity of membrane repolarization for sustained motoneuron firing.
source: In contrast to long (>50 ms) duration pulses (Figure 2d), motoneurons showed no signs of AP adaptation to pulse trains with brief (<5 ms) pulses, indicating the necessity of membrane repolarization for sustained motoneuron firing (Figure 3—figure supplement 3).
evidence: The claim is supported by reference to Figure 2d and Figure 3—figure supplement 3 showing the experimental data.

claim: Stimulation was reliable into the behaviorally relevant physiological range with train frequencies tested up to 110 Hz.
source: Stimulation was reliable into the behaviorally relevant physiological range (the PRR/fundamental frequency of toadfish vocalizations) with train frequencies tested up to 110 Hz.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data.

claim: The weak repolarization capability and low excitability of the motoneurons provide the means to prevent sustained AP firing, which would decrease the extent of firing synchrony and precision across the VMN population.
source: The weak repolarization capability and low excitability of the motoneurons thus provide the means to prevent sustained AP firing, which would decrease the extent of firing synchrony and precision across the VMN population.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the experimental observations.

claim: The presence of the HYP only at high antidromic stimulation amplitudes strongly suggested a network-dependent activation of the HYP.
source: The presence of the HYP only at high antidromic stimulation amplitudes, that is, high levels of motoneuron recruitment, strongly suggested a network-dependent activation of the HYP.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the experimental observations.

claim: Once close to the antidromic AP, an HYP started to appear that increased in amplitude the closer the contralateral-evoked potential came to the ipsilateral-evoked antidromic AP.
source: Once close to the antidromic AP, an HYP started to appear that increased in amplitude the closer the contralateral-evoked potential came to the ipsilateral-evoked antidromic AP (Figure 4b; heat map in Figure 4a; also see Video 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by reference to Figure 4a, 4b and Video 1 showing the experimental data.

claim: These experiments suggested that an increase in overall depolarization in the vocal network is needed to generate the HYP.
source: These experiments suggested that an increase in overall depolarization in the vocal network is needed to generate the HYP.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the experimental results.

claim: With decreasing lag between the antidromically evoked potential and the depolarization during the VOC, an HYP started to appear in the contralateral-evoked potential that increased in amplitude.
source: With decreasing lag between the antidromically evoked potential and the depolarization during the VOC, an HYP started to appear in the contralateral-evoked potential that increased in amplitude (Figure 4c, d).
evidence: The claim is supported by reference to Figure 4c, d showing the experimental data.

claim: This again showed the necessity of a network-wide depolarization in order to elicit the HYP.
source: This again showed the necessity of a network-wide depolarization in order to elicit the HYP.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the experimental results.

claim: After intracellular iontophoresis of QX314, motoneurons exhibited a small, but significant, decrease in AP amplitude compared to baseline conditions during VOCs (baseline: 31 ± 2.67 mV vs. QX314: 27.27 ± 2.53 mV; n = 7, N = 2; p=0.015).
source: After intracellular iontophoresis of QX314, motoneurons exhibited a small, but significant, decrease in AP amplitude compared to baseline conditions during VOCs (Figure 5a) (baseline: 31 ± 2.67 mV vs. QX314: 27.27 ± 2.53 mV; n = 7, N = 2; p=0.015).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data (p=0.015) and reference to Figure 5a.

claim: There was a much more prominent decrease in antidromically evoked AP amplitude relative to baseline after QX314 injection (baseline: 21.92 ± 7.16 mV vs. QX314: 8.90 ± 6.82 mV; n = 7, N = 2; p=0.006).
source: There was a much more prominent decrease in antidromically evoked AP amplitude relative to baseline (baseline: 21.92 ± 7.16 mV vs. QX314: 8.90 ± 6.82 mV; n = 7, N = 2; p=0.006) (Figure 5b).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data (p=0.006) and reference to Figure 5b.

claim: A significant difference in the HYP during VOCs was observed after QX314 injection (baseline: −9.87 ± 0.75 mV vs. QX314: −2.19 ± 0.95 mV; n = 7, N = 2; p=0.003).
source: While a significant difference in the HYP during VOCs was observed (baseline: −9.87 ± 0.75 mV vs. QX314: −2.19 ± 0.95 mV; n = 7, N = 2; p=0.003)
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data (p=0.003).

claim: No significant change could be detected in the HYP following antidromic activation after QX314 injection (baseline: −4.44 ± 3.57 mV vs. QX314: −4.3 ± 3.56 mV, n = 7, N = 2; p=0.703).
source: no significant change could be detected in the HYP following antidromic activation (baseline: −4.44 ± 3.57 mV vs. QX314: −4.3 ± 3.56 mV, n = 7, N = 2; p=0.703) (Figure 5a, b).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data (p=0.703) and reference to Figure 5a, b.

claim: The contribution of the recorded motoneuronal AP firing to the firing of that motoneuron is rather small during VOC activity (the activity of the neuron is dominated by gap junction-coupled potentials).
source: These experiments demonstrated that (i) the contribution of the recorded motoneuronal AP firing to the firing of that motoneuron is rather small during VOC activity (the activity of the neuron is dominated by gap junction-coupled potentials);
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the QX314 experimental results.

claim: During a VOC, the HYP amplitude of the recorded neuron only partly depends on its firing an AP.
source: (ii) during a VOC, the HYP amplitude of the recorded neuron only partly depends on its firing an AP (also see above);
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the QX314 experimental results.

claim: Most of the activity displayed by a given motoneuron reflects population-level motoneuronal activity.
source: and (iii) most of the activity displayed by a given motoneuron reflects population-level motoneuronal activity.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the QX314 experimental results.

claim: A combined superfusion and pressure injection of carbenoxolone (CBX) directly into VMN severely impaired the vocal network's ability to generate synchronized motor discharges as evidenced by barely detectable VOC activity.
source: A combined superfusion of the exposed vocal hindbrain region coupled with pressure injection of carbenoxolone (CBX, a gap junction blocker) directly into VMN severely impaired the vocal network's ability to generate synchronized motor discharges as evidenced by barely detectable VOC activity (Figure 5c, red trace).
evidence: The claim is supported by reference to Figure 5c showing the experimental data.

claim: Upon antidromic stimulation after CBX application, APs had a similar amplitude as they did in controls (baseline: 17.80 ± 2.05 mV vs. CBX: 16.15 ± 2.14 mV; n = 25, N = 3; p=0.59).
source: Upon antidromic stimulation (Figure 5d), APs had a similar amplitude as they did in controls (see violin plots in Figure 5d; baseline: 17.80 ± 2.05 mV vs. CBX: 16.15 ± 2.14 mV; n = 25, N = 3; p=0.59)
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data (p=0.59) and reference to Figure 5d.

claim: The loss of vocal-related activity during midbrain activation after CBX was not due to CBX impairment of motoneuron AP-generating capacity, but to decreased electrotonic input to the motoneurons.
source: showing that the loss of vocal-related activity during midbrain activation was not due to CBX impairment of motoneuron AP-generating capacity, but to decreased electrotonic input to the motoneurons.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the CBX experimental results.

claim: No HYP could be elicited in antidromic-activated motoneurons after CBX application (baseline: −4.79 ± 0.94 mV vs. CBX: −0.79 ± 0.97 mV; n = 25, N = 3; p<0.0001).
source: No HYP could be elicited in antidromic-activated motoneurons (baseline: −4.79 ± 0.94 mV vs. CBX: −0.79 ± 0.97 mV; n = 25, N = 3; p<0.0001).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data (p<0.0001).

claim: Gap junctional coupling is required to activate the HYP.
source: This showed that gap junctional coupling is indeed required to activate the HYP.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the CBX experimental results.

claim: SR-SIM imaging demonstrated dense, punctate glycinergic-immunoreactive labeling throughout VMN.
source: SR-SIM imaging demonstrated dense, punctate glycinergic-immunoreactive labeling throughout VMN.
evidence: The claim is supported by super-resolution microscopy data.

claim: Overlap of glycinergic signal with labeling for synaptic vesicle protein (SV2) revealed prominent boutons directly abutting motoneuron somata.
source: Overlap of glycinergic signal with labeling for synaptic vesicle protein (SV2) revealed prominent boutons directly abutting motoneuron somata (Figure 6a–c).
evidence: The claim is supported by reference to Figure 6a–c showing the microscopy data.

claim: Glycinergic boutons were also observed on motoneuron dendrites within the contralateral VMN and VPN.
source: Glycinergic boutons were also observed on motoneuron dendrites within the contralateral VMN (Figure 6d–h) and VPN (Figure 6d, i–k).
evidence: The claim is supported by reference to Figure 6d–k showing the microscopy data.

claim: These results demonstrated an anatomical basis for glycinergic release and inhibition spatially distributed across the entire somato-dendritic extent of vocal motoneurons.
source: These results demonstrated an anatomical basis for glycinergic release and inhibition spatially distributed across the entire somato-dendritic extent of vocal motoneurons.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the anatomical data.

claim: At midbrain stimulation levels sub-threshold to VOC compound potential induction, tonic membrane HYPs (on average −2.48 ± 0.68 mV below RMP; n = 7; N = 2) could be detected, indicating activation of inhibitory inputs.
source: We observed early on that at midbrain stimulation levels sub-threshold to VOC compound potential induction, tonic membrane HYPs (on average −2.48 ± 0.68 mV below RMP; n = 7; N = 2) could be detected, indicating activation of inhibitory inputs (Figure 7—figure supplement 1a, left; magenta trace: subthreshold, black trace: suprathreshold)
evidence: The claim is supported by reference to Figure 7—figure supplement 1a showing the experimental data.

claim: Changing the chloride reversal potential by intracellular chloride injections via 3 M KCl-filled electrodes revealed a prominent inhibitory input to motoneurons during VOCs.
source: We also found that changing the chloride reversal potential by intracellular chloride injections via 3 M KCl-filled electrodes revealed a prominent inhibitory input to motoneurons during VOCs as the membrane potential showed significant changes in the degree of repolarization compared to baseline levels (Figure 7—figure supplement 1b, blue arrow).
evidence: The claim is supported by reference to Figure 7—figure supplement 1b showing the experimental data.

claim: The HYP during VOCs was heavily reduced after chloride injection (baseline: −9.62 ± 1.34 mV vs. chloride injected: −1.20 ± 1.23 mV; n = 10, N = 3; p<0.001).
source: The HYP during VOCs was heavily reduced (baseline: −9.62 ± 1.34 mV vs. chloride injected: −1.20 ± 1.23 mV; n = 10, N = 3; p<0.001) (Figure 7—figure supplement 1b, blue trace), thus indicating an inhibitory contribution to vocal behavior.
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data (p<0.001) and reference to Figure 7—figure supplement 1b.

claim: Antidromic stimulation still showed the HYP after chloride injection, however, at a reduced amplitude (baseline: −5.28 ± 1.95 mV vs. chloride injected: −3.30 ± 1.71 mV; n = 9, N = 3; p=0.093).
source: Antidromic stimulation still showed the HYP, however, at a reduced amplitude (baseline: −5.28 ± 1.95 mV vs. chloride injected: −3.30 ± 1.71 mV; n = 9, N = 3; p=0.093) (Figure 7—figure supplement 1c).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data (p=0.093) and reference to Figure 7—figure supplement 1c.

claim: After strychnine injection, no change in AP amplitude during midbrain-evoked VOCs could be detected.
source: After strychnine injection, no change in AP amplitude during midbrain-evoked VOCs (Figure 7a) could be detected.
evidence: The claim is supported by reference to Figure 7a showing the experimental data.

claim: Strychnine abolished the HYP of motoneurons during VOCs (baseline −4.67 ± 1.88 mV vs. strychnine: 0.89 ± 1.88 mV, n = 20, N = 2; p<0.001).
source: Strychnine, however, abolished the HYP of motoneurons during VOCs (baseline −4.67 ± 1.88 mV vs. strychnine: 0.89 ± 1.88 mV, n = 20, N = 2; p<0.001) (Figure 7a).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data (p<0.001) and reference to Figure 7a.

claim: The HYP during antidromic stimulation completely disappeared after strychnine injection (baseline: −3.85 ± 0.86 mV vs. strychnine: 0.40 ± 0.86 mV, n = 20, N = 2; p<0.001).
source: The HYP during antidromic stimulation completely disappeared (baseline: −3.85 ± 0.86 mV vs. strychnine: 0.40 ± 0.86 mV, n = 20, N = 2; p<0.001) (Figure 7a, insets).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data (p<0.001) and reference to Figure 7a.

claim: These results suggested that glycinergic neurons, activated via gap junctional coupling, were responsible for generating the HYP during antidromic stimulation.
source: These results suggested that glycinergic neurons, activated via gap junctional coupling, were responsible for generating the HYP during antidromic stimulation.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the strychnine experimental results.

claim: Following strychnine injections, spontaneous VOCs appeared with similar decreases in motoneuron HYP amplitude not seen for spontaneous VOCs under control conditions without prior strychnine injections.
source: Following strychnine injections, spontaneous VOCs appeared with similar decreases in motoneuron HYP amplitude not seen for spontaneous VOCs under control conditions without prior strychnine injections (Figure 7c).
evidence: The claim is supported by reference to Figure 7c showing the experimental data.

claim: The results imply that gap junction coupling between motor and glycinergic VPN neurons is sufficient to drive AP firing of glycinergic neurons.
source: Since VMN motoneurons lack axon collaterals (Figure 1d), the results imply that gap junction coupling between motor and glycinergic VPN neurons is sufficient to drive AP firing of glycinergic neurons.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the strychnine experimental results and anatomical data, with reference to Figure 1d.

claim: The interval between the first and second motoneuron AP significantly decreased following strychnine application (baseline: 9.61 ± 0.69 ms, strychnine 7.94 ± 0.69 ms; n = 10, N = 2; p=0.049).
source: The interval between the first and second motoneuron AP significantly decreased following strychnine application (baseline: 9.61 ± 0.69 ms, strychnine 7.94 ± 0.69 ms; n = 10, N = 2; p=0.049).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data (p=0.049).

claim: Variability of the interspike interval (ISI), as measured by the coefficient of variation, increased significantly after strychnine application (baseline: 4.90 ± 3.95%, strychnine: 13.54 ± 3.95%; n = 10, N = 2; p=0.009).
source: Variability of the interspike interval (ISI), as measured by the coefficient of variation, also increased significantly (baseline: 4.90 ± 3.95%, strychnine: 13.54 ± 3.95%; n = 10, N = 2; p=0.009).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data (p=0.009).

claim: Strychnine increases both frequency and variability of motoneuron firing that matches VOC output.
source: Thus, strychnine increases both frequency and variability of motoneuron firing that matches VOC output.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the strychnine experimental results.

claim: Spontaneous VOCs following injection with strychnine had potentials varying in width and multiple peaks, reminiscent of VOCs associated with weak VMN synchronization.
source: Spontaneous VOCs following injection with strychnine had potentials varying in width (Figure 7c) and multiple peaks, reminiscent of VOCs associated with weak VMN synchronization (Figure 2b).
evidence: The claim is supported by reference to Figure 7c and Figure 2b showing the experimental data.

claim: The pattern of VPN activity directly predicts the pattern of VMN activity, the intervals of VOC potentials, and vocalization PRR.
source: The pattern of VPN activity directly predicts the pattern of VMN activity, the intervals of VOC potentials, and vocalization PRR (Figure 8a, Chagnaud et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Chagnaud et al., 2012 and reference to Figure 8a.

claim: Antidromic stimulation of the vocal nerve leads to membrane depolarizations (via electrotonic input) in premotor VPN neurons in the closely related midshipman.
source: Antidromic stimulation of the vocal nerve leads to membrane depolarizations (via electrotonic input) in premotor VPN neurons in the closely related midshipman (Bass and Baker, 1990).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Bass and Baker, 1990.

claim: Toadfish VPN neurons generate two depolarizing components, one before and one during VOCs, that might reflect motoneuron activity leaking through gap junctions.
source: Toadfish VPN neurons generate two depolarizing components, one before and one during VOCs, that might reflect motoneuron activity leaking through gap junctions (Figure 8a, Chagnaud and Bass, 2014).
evidence: The claim is based on speculation supported by citation to Chagnaud and Bass, 2014 and reference to Figure 8a.

claim: During antidromic stimulation of the vocal nerve, VPN neurons showed small subthreshold potentials similar to VMN neurons indicative of gap junctional coupling, as well as APs at higher stimulation amplitudes.
source: During antidromic stimulation of the vocal nerve, VPN neurons showed small subthreshold potentials similar to VMN neurons indicative of gap junctional coupling, as well as APs at higher stimulation amplitudes (Figure 8b).
evidence: The claim is supported by reference to Figure 8b showing the experimental data.

claim: Antidromic activation in motoneurons could elicit AP firing in VPN premotoneurons.
source: Thus, antidromic activation in motoneurons could elicit AP firing in VPN premotoneurons.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the experimental observations.

claim: The latency of VPN APs (ipsi: 4.66 ± 0.01 ms, n = 3; N = 1; contra: 5.43 ± 0.16 ms; n = 3; N = 1) roughly coincided with the depolarization following antidromically elicited APs in motoneurons.
source: The latency of these APs (ipsi: 4.66 ± 0.01 ms, n = 3; N = 1; contra: 5.43 ± 0.16 ms; n = 3; N = 1) roughly coincided with the depolarization following antidromically elicited APs in motoneurons (Figure 3a, magenta arrow).
evidence: The claim is supported by reference to Figure 3a showing the experimental data.

claim: A decrease in latency between the ipsilateral and contralateral stimulation pulses eventually led to AP firing in VPN neurons, showing that AP firing in VPN neurons also depends on gap junctional activation of the vocal network.
source: A decrease in latency between the ipsilateral and contralateral stimulation pulses eventually led to AP firing in VPN neurons, thus showing that AP firing in VPN neurons also depends on gap junctional activation of the vocal network (Figure 8c).
evidence: The claim is supported by reference to Figure 8c showing the experimental data.

claim: VPN activation could have led to motoneuron depolarization and activation of gap junction-coupled glycinergic neurons that, in turn, inhibit motoneurons and generated the HYP.
source: VPN activation could thus have led to motoneuron depolarization (Figure 3, magenta arrows) and activation of gap junction-coupled glycinergic neurons (Rosner et al., 2018) that, in turn, inhibit motoneurons and generated the HYP.
evidence: The claim is based on speculation supported by citation to Rosner et al., 2018 and reference to Figure 3.

claim: Our experiments support the hypothesis that gap junction-mediated activation of glycinergic neurons can account for remarkable synchrony in motoneuron firing and likely also contributes to pattern generation.
source: Together, our experiments support the hypothesis that gap junction-mediated activation of glycinergic neurons can account for remarkable synchrony in motoneuron firing and likely also contributes to pattern generation.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the aggregate experimental results.

claim: Teleost families with evidence for soniferous behavior contain nearly two-thirds of actinopterygian species.
source: Teleost families with evidence for soniferous behavior contain nearly two-thirds of actinopterygian species (Rice et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Rice et al., 2020.

claim: Concurrent activation of neurons required for rapid and precise activation of muscle groups underlying acoustic signaling in different lineages of fishes and in tetrapods might all benefit from gap junction-mediated glycinergic inhibition.
source: Concurrent activation of neurons required for rapid and precise activation of muscle groups underlying acoustic signaling in different lineages of fishes (Chagnaud et al., 2012; Kéver et al., 2020) and in tetrapods (Mead et al., 2017; Kwong-Brown et al., 2019) might all benefit from gap junction-mediated glycinergic inhibition.
evidence: The claim is based on speculation supported by citations to Chagnaud et al., 2012; Kéver et al., 2020; Mead et al., 2017; Kwong-Brown et al., 2019.

claim: An important and novel role of gap junctional coupling in the toadfish vocal network is its involvement in generating the prominent HYP in toadfish motoneurons detected during both midbrain-evoked VOCs and antidromic motoneuron stimulation.
source: An important and novel role of gap junctional coupling in the toadfish vocal network is its involvement in generating the prominent HYP in toadfish motoneurons detected during both midbrain-evoked VOCs and antidromic motoneuron stimulation.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the experimental results.

claim: The HYP is essential to generating vocalizations with high temporal precision.
source: This HYP, which could not be elicited upon intracellular current injection, is essential to generating vocalizations with high temporal precision.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the experimental results.

claim: A distinguishing temporal feature between grunts and boatwhistles is the greater stability of time intervals between successive sound pulses in boatwhistles.
source: A distinguishing temporal feature between grunts and boatwhistles, the two main call types of toadfishes, is the greater stability of time intervals between successive sound pulses in boatwhistles (Maruska and Mensinger, 2009)
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Maruska and Mensinger, 2009.

claim: Our results strongly imply a salient role for glycinergic premotoneurons in determining the temporal feature of toadfish calls that varies with social context (aggression versus courtship).
source: Our results strongly imply a salient role for glycinergic premotoneurons in determining this temporal feature of toadfish calls that varies with social context (aggression versus courtship).
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the experimental results.

claim: For fish of both sexes collected during the non-breeding season, the HYP did not appear during antidromic stimulation, although it was present during the VOC.
source: Interestingly, for fish of both sexes collected during the non-breeding season, the HYP did not appear during antidromic stimulation, although it was present during the VOC (not shown).
evidence: The claim is based on observations from the experimental data.

claim: A seasonal variability in the expression of the HYP upon antidromic stimulation appeared to be present.
source: While we did not quantify this result, a seasonal variability in the expression of the HYP upon antidromic stimulation appeared to be present.
evidence: The claim is based on observations from the experimental data.

claim: This variation might be due to the previously observed seasonal variability in expression levels of connexin transcripts in the closely related midshipman fish.
source: This variation might be due to the previously observed seasonal variability in expression levels of connexin transcripts in the closely related midshipman fish (Feng et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is based on speculation supported by citation to Feng et al., 2015.

claim: During natural vocal behavior, VPN would be feeding forward to VMN, given that VPN fires before VMN during VOCs.
source: During natural vocal behavior, VPN would be feeding forward to VMN, given that VPN fires before VMN during VOCs (Bass and Baker, 1990; Chagnaud et al., 2011; Chagnaud and Bass, 2014).
evidence: The claim is based on inference supported by citations to Bass and Baker, 1990; Chagnaud et al., 2011; Chagnaud and Bass, 2014.

claim: Excitatory VPN neurons could activate VPN's glycinergic neurons, via electrotonic coupling, before the motoneurons.
source: Consequently, excitatory VPN neurons could activate VPN's glycinergic neurons, via elecrotonic coupling, before the motoneurons (Figure 9).
evidence: The claim is based on speculation with reference to Figure 9.

claim: Electrotonic coupling of VPN excitatory neurons to glycinergic VPN neurons most likely activates the latter, which causes feed-forward inhibitory action upon motoneurons.
source: Electrotonic coupling of VPN excitatory neurons to glycinergic VPN neurons thus most likely activates the latter, which causes feed-forward inhibitory action upon motoneurons.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the experimental results.

claim: Anatomical evidence for local activation within VPN comes from transneuronal labeling of local VPN neurons after filling an intracellulary-recorded VPN neuron with neurobiotin.
source: Anatomical evidence for local activation within VPN comes from transneuronal labeling of local VPN neurons after filling an intracellulary-recorded VPN neuron with neurobiotin (Chagnaud et al., 2011; Chagnaud and Bass, 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Chagnaud et al., 2011 and Chagnaud and Bass, 2014.

claim: Inhibitory action in this network can serve multiple functions: it repolarizes motoneurons, a feature essential to VMN's ability to repetitively fire APs, and it generates a window of decreased excitability that prevents motoneuron misfiring outside of the VPN rhythm.
source: Inhibitory action in this network can serve multiple functions. First, it repolarizes motoneurons, a feature essential to VMN's ability to repetitively fire APs, as seen by our pulse train experiments. Second, it generates a window of decreased excitability that prevents motoneuron misfiring outside of the VPN rhythm due to the long time course of inhibitory action compared to the normal activation rhythm of ca. 100 Hz (see Video 2).
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the experimental results with reference to Video 2.

claim: A gap junction-mediated, feed-forward glycinergic inhibition could account for temporal patterning in the millisecond time range that characterizes the vocal network and behavior of toadfishes.
source: A gap junction-mediated, feed-forward glycinergic inhibition could account for temporal patterning in the millisecond time range that characterizes the vocal network and behavior of toadfishes (Pappas and Bennett, 1966; Bass and Baker, 1991; Chagnaud et al., 2011; Chagnaud et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is based on inference supported by citations to Pappas and Bennett, 1966; Bass and Baker, 1991; Chagnaud et al., 2011; Chagnaud et al., 2012.

claim: A similar mechanism has previously been shown for the Mauthner cell escape circuit.
source: A similar mechanism has previously been shown for the Mauthner cell escape circuit (Furukawa and Furshpan, 1963; Diamond and Roper, 1973; Diamond et al., 1973; Faber et al., 1989; Zottoli and Faber, 2000; Korn and Faber, 2005; Sillar, 2009)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Furukawa and Furshpan, 1963; Diamond and Roper, 1973; Diamond et al., 1973; Faber et al., 1989; Zottoli and Faber, 2000; Korn and Faber, 2005; Sillar, 2009.

claim: This mechanism may operate in other vocal systems in teleosts and tetrapods that are dependent on comparable levels of temporal precision.
source: and may operate in other vocal systems in teleosts and tetrapods that are dependent on comparable levels of temporal precision (Sturdy et al., 2003; Rome, 2006; Bass et al., 2015; Mead et al., 2017; Nelson et al., 2018; Kwong-Brown et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is based on speculation supported by citations to Sturdy et al., 2003; Rome, 2006; Bass et al., 2015; Mead et al., 2017; Nelson et al., 2018; Kwong-Brown et al., 2019.

claim: We hypothesize that the characteristic 'pacemaker' potential that leads to VPN oscillatory-like activity in midshipman originates from motor–premotor coupling.
source: While we do not directly show the effect of motoneuronal activity back-propagating through gap junctions on the VPN firing pattern, we hypothesize that the characteristic 'pacemaker' potential that leads to VPN oscillatory-like activity in midshipman (Chagnaud et al., 2011) originates from motor–premotor coupling.
evidence: The claim is based on speculation supported by citation to Chagnaud et al., 2011.

claim: Excitatory potentials from the VMN network are shunted by the presumed feed-forward inhibitory action, while the inhibitory potentials would be allowed to travel through gap junctions to contribute to VPN patterning.
source: This would mean that excitatory potentials from the VMN network are shunted by the presumed feed-forward inhibitory action, while the inhibitory potentials would be allowed to travel through gap junctions to contribute to VPN patterning (e.g., see Figure 8a; also see Chagnaud et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is based on speculation with reference to Figure 8a and citation to Chagnaud et al., 2011.

claim: It is conceivable that the gap junctional coupling between VPN and VMN neurons also affects VPN activity and is another example of how premotor and motor neurons interact to generate motor patterns.
source: It is, however, conceivable that the gap junctional coupling between VPN and VMN neurons also affects VPN activity and is another example of how premotor and motor neurons interact to generate motor patterns (Barkan and Zornik, 2019).
evidence: The claim is based on speculation supported by citation to Barkan and Zornik, 2019.

claim: Temporal precision in motoneuronal output from the toadfish vocal network depends on gap junction-mediated, glycinergic inhibition, resulting in a reduced probability of motoneuron activation manifested as a prominent HYP that guards against motoneuron misfiring.
source: We provide evidence that temporal precision in motoneuronal output from the toadfish vocal network depends on gap junction-mediated, glycinergic inhibition, resulting in a reduced probability of motoneuron activation manifested as a prominent HYP that guards against motoneuron misfiring.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the aggregate experimental results.

claim: Together with the activation of excitatory VPN neurons, the phasic inhibition provides an essential mechanism for generating rapid, highly phasic acoustic modulations determining vocal PRR.
source: Together with the activation of excitatory VPN neurons, the phasic inhibition provides an essential mechanism for generating rapid, highly phasic acoustic modulations determining vocal PRR.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the experimental results.

claim: Teleost auditory systems are exquisitely adapted to temporal coding, including the PRR and fundamental frequency of vocal signals.
source: From a sensory-motor coupling perspective, teleost auditory systems are exquisitely adapted to temporal coding, including the PRR and fundamental frequency of vocal signals (Bass and McKibben, 2003b; Fay and Edds-Walton, 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Bass and McKibben, 2003b and Fay and Edds-Walton, 2008.

claim: The vocal and auditory systems 'co-evolved and we should expect them to share the same underlying code for signal generation and recognition'.
source: As Capranica (Capranica, 1992) wrote, the vocal and auditory systems 'co-evolved and we should expect them to share the same underlying code for signal generation and recognition'.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Capranica, 1992.

claim: Call types differing in temporal properties, including PRR, indicate behavioral state.
source: From a behavioral perspective, call types differing in temporal properties, including PRR, indicate behavioral state.
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge in the field.

claim: Brief, broadband signals with variable PRRs such as grunts inform conspecifics of an aggressive state during defense of resources such as nest sites.
source: For example, brief, broadband signals with variable PRRs such as grunts (see Figure 1a) inform conspecifics of an aggressive state during defense of resources such as nest sites
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge in the field with reference to Figure 1a.

claim: Multiharmonic advertisement calls with a more stable PRR like the boatwhistle can function as courtship signals, indicating readiness to mate.
source: whereas mutliharmonic advertisement calls with a more stable PRR (i.e., F0) like the boatwhistle (Figure 1a) can function as courtship signals, indicating readiness to mate (for reviews, see Bass and McKibben, 2003b; Ladich et al., 2006).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Bass and McKibben, 2003b and Ladich et al., 2006, with reference to Figure 1a.

claim: Underwater playbacks show that toadfishes, including Gulf toadfish, distinguish call types and PRRs.
source: Underwater playbacks further show that toadfishes, including Gulf toadfish, distinguish call types and PRRs (Fish, 1972; Winn, 1972; McKibben and Bass, 1998; McKibben and Bass, 2001; Remage-Healey and Bass, 2005).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Fish, 1972; Winn, 1972; McKibben and Bass, 1998; McKibben and Bass, 2001; Remage-Healey and Bass, 2005.

claim: Individual differences in boatwhistle PRR are linked to male quality and aggressive state in the Lusitanian toadfish, Halobatrachus didactylus.
source: Individual differences in boatwhistle PRR are further linked to male quality and aggressive state in the Lusitanian toadfish, Halobatrachus didactylus (Vasconcelos et al., 2012; Amorim et al., 2015b).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Vasconcelos et al., 2012 and Amorim et al., 2015b.

claim: Behavioral evidence supports a role for PRR in individual and species recognition in other soniferous teleosts.
source: More broadly, behavioral evidence supports a role for PRR in individual and species recognition in other soniferous teleosts (Gerald, 1971; Myrberg and Spires, 1972; Myrberg and Riggio, 1985; Maruska et al., 2007; Amorim et al., 2015a).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Gerald, 1971; Myrberg and Spires, 1972; Myrberg and Riggio, 1985; Maruska et al., 2007; Amorim et al., 2015a.

claim: Transmission distance is limited by the frequency content of calls in shallow water habitats like those where toadfishes and other teleosts defend nests and engage in acoustic courtship.
source: As regards sound properties in water, transmission distance is limited by the frequency content of calls in shallow water habitats like those where toadfishes and other teleosts defend nests and engage in acoustic courtship (Gerald, 1971; Fine and Lenhardt, 1983; Bass and Clark, 2003a).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Gerald, 1971; Fine and Lenhardt, 1983; Bass and Clark, 2003a.

claim: The principal limitation to call PRR and F0 in species like toadfishes that generate calls with frequency content mainly below 500 Hz is muscle contraction rate that determines swim bladder vibration rate.
source: The principal limitation to call PRR and F0 in species like toadfishes that generate calls with frequency content mainly below 500 Hz is muscle contraction rate that determines swim bladder vibration rate.
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge in the field.

claim: A superfast motor system, driven by a central network that directly determines high temporal precision in synchronous activation of muscle fibers to maximize call amplitude as well as PRR and F0, enhances transmission distance.
source: A superfast motor system, driven by a central network that directly determines high temporal precision in synchronous activation of muscle fibers to maximize call amplitude as well as PRR and F0, enhances transmission distance.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the experimental results and established knowledge.

claim: While a combination of mechanisms increase temporal precision in the time domain, gap junction-mediated, phasic glycinergic inhibition provides an effective means to achieve temporal precision in motor coding at a network level.
source: While a combination of mechanisms increase temporal precision in the time domain, gap junction-mediated, phasic glycinergic inhibition provides an effective means to achieve temporal precision in motor coding at a network level.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the experimental results.

claim: Detection of vocalization fine structure including PRR is a salient feature of communication in many tetrapods.
source: Detection of vocalization fine structure including PRR is also a salient feature of communication in many tetrapods (Gerhardt et al., 2007; Rose, 2014), including some non-human primates (Hauser et al., 1998).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Gerhardt et al., 2007; Rose, 2014; Hauser et al., 1998.

claim: Studies of motor coding in tetrapods using nerve or extracellular recordings, or electromyography, support a role for the hindbrain in determining rapid acoustic events.
source: Studies of motor coding in tetrapods using nerve or extracellular recordings, or electromyography, also support a role for the hindbrain in determining rapid acoustic events (see Chagnaud et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Chagnaud et al., 2011.

claim: We expect mechanisms comparable to those reported here for preventing motoneuron misfiring to be present in other lineages of vocal vertebrates.
source: We expect mechanisms comparable to those reported here for preventing motoneuron misfiring that, in general, could disrupt distinct transitions in acoustic waveforms to be present in other lineages of vocal vertebrates as well.
evidence: The claim is based on speculation.

claim: These mechanisms may contribute to time coding in other motor systems requiring high levels of precision.
source: Even more broadly, they may contribute to time coding in other motor systems requiring high levels of precision.
evidence: The claim is based on speculation.

claim: Both sexes of Gulf toadfish are capable of acoustic signaling.
source: Though field studies mainly characterize male vocalization, both sexes are capable of acoustic signaling (e.g., Demski and Gerald, 1972; Remage-Healey and Bass, 2005; Fine and Thorson, 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Demski and Gerald, 1972; Remage-Healey and Bass, 2005; Fine and Thorson, 2008.

claim: Both sexes produce grunts, but only males are known to produce boatwhistles.
source: Both sexes produce grunts, but only males are known to produce boatwhistles (Winn, 1967; Winn, 1972; Thorson and Fine, 2002).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Winn, 1967; Winn, 1972; Thorson and Fine, 2002.
